name: Nasmi

anatomy.part: far end of the laid rope, where the twist still holds
the rope body near its tip, where the lay begins to loosen
the knot where the strands part, the brightest point of the fray
the end of the first loose strand, trailing down
a bend in the long lower strand
a second bend further along the same strand
the tip of a strand flung far to the east
the final hair of the outermost strand

myth: When Aun cut the string, the sky went up, and the dead went with it as kites. But the Unflown lies past where the wind comes back, and there the dead do not stay knotted. Mother Hesk counted them as they left, and the count was right, but what she could not count was the rope. Nasmi is a length of old rope, untwisted back to its fibres, each strand going its own road. The sailors who saw it in the south say the strands never reach one another again. Each one is a voice that goes on alone, thin and cold, singing in the tar-smelling dark. Ennu, who wrights kites from cloth and bone, once tried to lay the strands back. His hands cramped and he gave it up, and that is why the old women say: do not untwist what you are sad to lose. Keep your knots tied, and keep counting.
verse:
Hands untwist the rope,
each strand takes its own far road,
no knot remembers.
